format: F10 The Paradox + F7 Follow the Thing

beats.say: April, in the onion fields of Maharashtra, in western India. A farmer pulls up an onion.
A few months earlier, in December twenty twenty-three, India had banned the export of this vegetable.
Not rice. Not wheat. Onions. And the government said the ban was to protect consumers at home.
But its own price fund says that at harvest time, onion prices normally fall steeply. And as stored stocks run down, they climb.
So the same bulb can be cheap when it comes out of the ground, and dear a few months later. In the same year.
How can both be true?
We read the agriculture ministry's crop tables, the government's trade notices, and the Election Commission's results. And three things you may have heard about the onion need a closer look.
The answer is not inside the onion. It is in the map behind it.
First, the onion itself. An old Ayurvedic text, the Charaka Samhita, already describes it, and calls it good with food.
Yet some kitchens leave it out on purpose. A Jain community website explains that pulling up a root kills the whole plant, and many tiny lives with it.
So many Jains avoid onion, some more strictly than others. And in some Hindu traditions, onion and garlic count as over-stimulating, and are left out.
Essential in one kitchen, avoided in another. But none of that explains why its price can shake a country. For that, you need a map.
In twenty twenty-four to twenty-five, India grew nearly thirty-one million tonnes of onions.
By the count of the UN's food agency, India grew more dry onions than any other country in twenty twenty-three. In its figures for the next year, China edges just ahead.
So you might think a crop that big grows all over the country. Look where it grows.
One state, Maharashtra, grew forty-four percent of it.
And almost half of all the land under onions in India is in that one state.
Add Madhya Pradesh and Karnataka, and three states grow two thirds of India's onions.
Maharashtra does not lead because its fields grow the most. Farms in Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat get far more from each hectare.
Maharashtra leads because it plants so much.
So the first thing you may have heard is wrong. India eats onions everywhere. It does not grow them everywhere.
And in that one state, zoom in to Nashik district.
But to see why prices swing, it is not enough to ask where onions grow. You have to ask when.
India grows onions in three seasons.
One crop is planted with the monsoon and comes out from October to December. Another comes out from January to March.
And then the big one. The spring crop, called rabi, harvested from the end of March to May.
ICAR, the government's farm research council, says the rabi crop is about sixty percent of India's onions.
So most of the year's onions arrive in a few months of spring. And they have to last.
ICAR says the stored rabi crop feeds the country until October or November. A clock of about six months.
They are kept in ventilated stores like this, open to the air.
And a stored onion is still alive. It breathes, and it loses water. Temperature and humidity decide how fast it rots, or starts to sprout.
ICAR says thirty to forty percent of the crop is lost in storage.
In its own trial, after a hundred and twenty days, ordinary ventilated storage had lost about fifty-five percent.
So every spring, a farmer here faces the same choice. Sell now, when harvest prices tend to fall. Or store, and hope the price rises faster than the heap shrinks.
Cold storage cuts the loss. But the same research page says the onions sprout soon after they come out of the cold.
So here is the dangerous gap. By autumn, the spring stock is running low. And the next crop is still in the ground, through the monsoon.
If that crop is late, little is left to bridge the gap. In December twenty twenty-three, a delayed crop was one of the reasons the government gave for its export ban.
From the stores, onions go to auction. Lasalgaon, in Nashik district, is one of the country's key onion markets, the government says.
You may have heard it called Asia's biggest onion market. We did not find that title in the government records we read, or on the market's own home page.
So the second thing you may have heard has no source we could find.
Remember the farmer's choice in April? Whatever he chose, his onions now face a long road.
To Delhi, it is about a thousand kilometres in a straight line. To Guwahati, nearly twice that.
So the government has put onions on trains. Yes: onions have their own train. It is called the Kanda Express.
In twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, eighty-six trainloads carried around eighty-eight thousand tonnes, to sixteen cities. More than seven times the year before.
These are onions the government bought and stored itself. In August twenty twenty-six, it announced it would sell them at thirty-five rupees a kilo.
The average retail price across India was then about thirty-eight. The state is moving onions across the map, to flatten the price.
Some onions leave India altogether. In twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, India exported about one and a half million tonnes.
To Malaysia, the UAE, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh, and more.
That is only about one onion in twenty that India grows. But for a government watching prices at home, it is a lever.
In October twenty twenty-three, it set a minimum export price of eight hundred dollars a tonne.
In December, it banned exports outright.
Even then, some onions went out, to governments that asked. Bangladesh was allowed fifty thousand tonnes.
In May twenty twenty-four, exports reopened, with a minimum price of five hundred and fifty dollars a tonne, and a forty percent export duty.
In September, the minimum price went, and the duty was cut to twenty percent. From April twenty twenty-five, the duty went too.
The trade ministry's list of notices, which we checked up to November twenty twenty-six, shows no new onion export order since.
And look at Bangladesh. In twenty twenty-three to twenty-four, a year of limits, it was still India's biggest buyer: over seven hundred thousand tonnes.
In twenty twenty-five to twenty-six, under ninety thousand. The trade figures do not say why.
For a grower in Maharashtra, Dhaka or Dubai is just another market. For a government watching prices in Delhi, the same shipment can look like supply leaving the country.
Why would a government watch onion prices so closely? Go back to nineteen ninety-eight.
In August that year, a newspaper reported that the commerce minister had ordered a temporary ban on onion exports, and that imports would be considered if prices stayed high.
A few months later, Delhi voted for its assembly.
In nineteen ninety-three, the BJP had won forty-nine of the seventy seats. In nineteen ninety-eight, Congress won fifty-two, and the BJP fifteen.
So did onions bring down a government? A study by three researchers notes that most accounts blame onion prices for the defeat.
But an election has many causes, and no record we read can measure the onion's share. So the third thing you may have heard is only half true.
What the same study did measure is stranger. It looked at weekly food prices in twenty-eight cities, and found an election pattern in just one food of the sixteen. The onion.
Onion prices tended to fall as a state election came near, and to rise after it. The authors point to a trade held in a few hands, but call their evidence only suggestive.
So, back to the question from the start. How can the onion be cheap and dear in the same year?
In spring, the rabi harvest pours into the markets. The price fund's own rules say a steep fall at harvest time is normal.
In March twenty twenty-five, as the new crop came in, the government said mandi prices across India had fallen thirty-nine percent. Shop prices fell ten percent over the month.
Remember the farmer's choice? Sell now, while harvest prices fall. Or store, and watch the heap get lighter every week.
Then the stored stock runs down, and the same rules say prices rise. If the next crop is late, families in the cities pay more.
So the government tries to be the store. It buys onions when there are many, and sells them when there are few.
From the rabi crop of twenty twenty-four, it bought about four hundred and seventy thousand tonnes.
And every tool is a choice between two groups. A ban is meant to protect buyers at home. But each onion kept in is one its grower cannot sell abroad.
So the onion's power does not come from the bulb. It comes from the map behind it.
Half the onion land, in one state.
Most of the crop, from one spring.
Months in stores, where it slowly shrinks.
A long road to the cities. And a border that opens and shuts.
And at the end of all that, one onion, pulled from a field in Maharashtra in April, lands in a pan in a city kitchen.
India's onion paradox is really a geography paradox.
